propositions.text: The Lougheed Building was designated a Municipal Historic Resource under the HRA and LBI agreed to rehabilitate it for Incentive Payments.
propositions.quote: At the centre of this appeal is the Lougheed Building in downtown Calgary, which was designated a “Municipal Historic Resource” under the Historical Resources Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. H-9 (“HRA”). The owner at the time of the designation, Lougheed Block Inc. (“LBI”), agreed to rehabilitate the building and adhere to certain restrictions on its use in exchange for 15 yearly payments (“Incentive Payments”) from the City of Calgary (“City”) totalling $3.4 million.

propositions.text: The Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title to the land pursuant to the HRA.
propositions.quote: That agreement was registered by caveat on title to the land pursuant to the HRA.

paragraphs.summary: The Lougheed Building was designated a Municipal Historic Resource; LBI agreed to rehabilitate it for Incentive Payments registered on title under the HRA, says the court.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns whether Incentive Payments run with the land, were sold in judicial sale, and the effect of assignments.
propositions.quote: This appeal involves a dispute between one of LBI’s creditors, Heritage Capital Corporation (“Heritage”), and the present owner of the Lougheed Building, 604 1st Street S.W. Inc. (“604”), both of which claim a right to the Incentive Payments. At issue is whether the Incentive Payments constitute a positive covenant running with the land by virtue of the HRA, whether they were sold in the judicial sale of the Lougheed Building, and what the present-day effect is of a number of agreements assigning an interest in the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal concerns whether Incentive Payments run with the land, were sold in judicial sale, and the effect of assignments, says the court.

propositions.text: Master and chambers judge found Incentive Payments did not run with the land and were not sold to 604; declined to decide priority.
propositions.quote: The master in chambers and the chambers judge both found that the Incentive Payments did not run with the land by operation of the HRA and that they had not been sold to 604 in the judicial sale. They declined to decide the issue of priority.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal found HRA creates sui generis covenants displacing common law rule; Incentive Payments run with the land.
propositions.quote: The majority of the Court of Appeal disagreed, finding that the HRA creates sui generis covenants that displace the common law rule that positive covenants do not run with the land. They accordingly held that the Incentive Payments ran with the land.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. dissenting would adopt chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A., dissenting, would have adopted the chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA.

paragraphs.summary: Master and chambers judge found Incentive Payments did not run with land and were not sold; Court of Appeal majority disagreed; O’Brien J.A. dissented, says court.

propositions.text: Allow appeal; only covenants in favour of persons listed in s.29(1) run with land under HRA, not Incentive Payments.
propositions.quote: We would allow the appeal. Even though, at s. 29(3), the HRA provides that a condition or covenant relating to the preservation or restoration of any land or building that is registered on title under s. 29(2) runs with the land and can be enforced whether it is positive or negative, we conclude that the only covenants that run with the land under the HRA are those that are in favour of the person or organizations listed in s. 29(1).

propositions.text: In this case, although City is listed, the covenant to pay Incentive Payments is not in its favour; thus payments do not run with land.
propositions.quote: In the instant case, although the City falls under the listed organizations, the covenant to pay the Incentive Payments is not in its favour. Therefore, the Incentive Payments do not run with the land under the HRA.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement shows no intention for Incentive Payments to run with the land.
propositions.quote: In any event, the Incentive Agreement between LBI and the City shows no intention for the Incentive Payments to run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal, finds only covenants in favour of listed persons run with land; payments not in City's favour and do not run with land; no intention to run with land.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments were not sold in judicial sale; no indication court or 604 intended to sell or buy them.
propositions.quote: We further conclude that the Incentive Payments were not sold in the judicial sale of the Lougheed Building. There was no indication, express or otherwise, in any of the documents related to the sale that the court intended to sell, or 604 intended to buy, the Incentive Payments.

propositions.text: Granting payments to 604 would create undeserved windfall and lack commercial rationale.
propositions.quote: Granting the payments to 604 as the current owner would create an undeserved windfall and would have no commercial rationale.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments assigned as security; priority governed by PPSA; remit priority issue to master in chambers.
propositions.quote: Lastly, we find that the Incentive Payments were assigned as security and that the order of priorities is therefore governed by the Personal Property Security Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. P-7 (“PPSA”). To the extent that the parties disagree about the effect of the PPSA, we would remit the matter to a master in chambers for determination on the priority issue alone.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Incentive Payments not sold in judicial sale; granting to 604 would be windfall; payments assigned as security with priority under PPSA; remit priority issue.

propositions.text: LBI acquired the Lougheed Building in 2003 and owned it when designated a Municipal Historic Resource in 2004.
propositions.quote: LBI acquired the Lougheed Building in 2003. It owned the building at the time it was designated a “Municipal Historic Resource” under s. 26 of the HRA in a bylaw passed by the City in 2004.

propositions.text: LBI and the City entered into the Incentive Agreement in 2006 for rehabilitation work and payments.
propositions.quote: Following the designation, LBI and the City entered into the Incentive Agreement in 2006. It provided that LBI would carry out rehabilitation work on the building and that, upon completion of the work, the City would begin paying LBI $3.4 million in Incentive Payments, in 15 annual instalments.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments aimed to compensate LBI for loss of economic value and rehabilitation expenses.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the Incentive Payments was twofold: to satisfy, pursuant to s. 28 of the HRA, all of LBI’s rights to compensation from the City for the loss of economic value sustained as a result of the passage of the designating bylaw and to compensate LBI for expenses incurred in carrying out the rehabilitation work.

propositions.text: Rehabilitation work restored the building to its 1912 appearance, completed in 2007, after which payments began.
propositions.quote: This work was required to repair the building and restore it to its original appearance of 1912. LBI completed the rehabilitation work in 2007 and started receiving the Incentive Payments shortly thereafter.

paragraphs.summary: The court states LBI acquired the building in 2003, was designated historic in 2004, entered an Incentive Agreement in 2006 for rehabilitation and payments, completed work in 2007, and began receiving payments.

propositions.text: The Incentive Agreement imposed use restrictions: commercial use only until all payments made, and maintaining performance space in the Grand Theatre.
propositions.quote: The Incentive Agreement also imposed certain restrictions on the owner of the Lougheed Building, namely: 8.4 The Building and Land shall be used for commercial purposes and no other purpose until all Yearly Installments have been paid pursuant to this Agreement. 8.5 The Owner shall use its best efforts to ensure that performance space is maintained within that portion of the Building that is currently referred to as the Grand Theatre.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Incentive Agreement restricted the building's use to commercial purposes and required maintaining performance space in the Grand Theatre.

propositions.text: Clause 8.3 stipulated the Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title with the entire agreement attached as a schedule.
propositions.quote: As was stipulated in clause 8.3, the Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title to the land. The entire agreement was attached to the caveat as a schedule.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Incentive Agreement was registered by caveat on title with the full agreement attached.

propositions.text: In 2006, LBI borrowed from Equitable, secured by mortgage, security agreement, and assignments including the Incentive Agreement (Equitable Assignment).
propositions.quote: In November 2006, LBI borrowed money from The Equitable Trust Company, since continued as the Equitable Bank (“Equitable”). The loan was secured by a mortgage, a general security agreement, and assignments of a range of agreements, including the Incentive Agreement (collectively the “Equitable Assignment”).

propositions.text: Equitable filed a financing statement at the Personal Property Registry then.
propositions.quote: Equitable filed a financing statement at the Personal Property Registry at that time.

propositions.text: In May 2007, LBI got more financing from Heritage and assigned Incentive Payments to Heritage as loan security (Heritage Assignment).
propositions.quote: In May 2007, LBI obtained additional financing from Heritage, and also assigned its right to the Incentive Payments to Heritage as security for the loan (the “Heritage Assignment”).

propositions.text: LBI defaulted on Equitable loan in May 2009; Equitable sued in June 2009 to enforce security.
propositions.quote: In May 2009, LBI defaulted on the Equitable loan, and in June 2009, Equitable commenced an action to enforce some of its security.

propositions.text: The Lougheed Building was advertised for judicial sale in March 2010; 604’s parent company offered to buy in June 2010; sale confirmed July 2010.
propositions.quote: The Lougheed Building was advertised for judicial sale in March 2010. In June 2010, 604’s parent company presented an offer to buy the property (the “604 Offer”), which was accepted in July 2010 by means of an “Order Confirming Sale” issued by the Court of Queen’s Bench.

paragraphs.summary: The court states LBI borrowed from Equitable in 2006 with security including the Incentive Agreement; later borrowed from Heritage assigning payments; defaulted; building was judicially sold to 604 in 2010.

propositions.text: In August 2010, LBI applied for declaration that Incentive Payments were not an interest in land and not sold to 604.
propositions.quote: Towards the end of August 2010, shortly before the sale’s closing date, LBI applied to a master in chambers for a declaration that the Incentive Payments were not an interest in land and were not included in the assets being sold to 604.

propositions.text: The master adjourned the application without deciding, allowing the sale to close on September 1, 2010, without prejudice to rights on the Incentive Payments issue.
propositions.quote: After hearing the parties’ submissions, the master adjourned the application without deciding the issue, on the condition that the transaction would close as scheduled on September 1, 2010, without prejudice to the parties’ rights on the issue of entitlement to the Incentive Payments.

propositions.text: After closing, Equitable assigned its interest in the Incentive Agreement to 604 (604 Assignment).
propositions.quote: After the closing, Equitable executed a specific assignment of its interest in the Incentive Agreement to 604 (the “604 Assignment”).

propositions.text: Heritage Assignment was registered at the Personal Property Registry in October 2010; no evidence 604 Assignment was registered before Heritage Assignment.
propositions.quote: The Heritage Assignment was only registered at the Personal Property Registry in October 2010. There is no evidence on the record in this Court that the 604 Assignment was registered at the Personal Property Registry before the Heritage Assignment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states LBI sought declaration that Incentive Payments were not land interest or sold; master adjourned; after sale Equitable assigned interest to 604; Heritage Assignment registered later than 604 Assignment.

propositions.text: 604 submits that Incentive Payments constitute a positive covenant running with the land due to registration under s. 29 of the HRA.
propositions.quote: In 604’s submission, as a result of the registration of the entire Incentive Agreement on title pursuant to s. 29 of the HRA, the Incentive Payments also constitute a positive covenant running with the land to which 604 is entitled as the new owner of the Lougheed Building.

propositions.text: Alternatively, 604 argues the Incentive Payments were assets sold in the judicial sale.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, 604 submits that the Incentive Payments were among the assets sold in the judicial sale.

propositions.text: It is undisputed that 604 is subject to covenants in clauses 8.4 and 8.5 restricting building use.
propositions.quote: It is undisputed that 604, as the owner of the Lougheed Building, is subject to the covenants in favour of the City set out in clauses 8.4 and 8.5 of the Incentive Agreement, which restrict the building’s use.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues Incentive Payments run with the land under s. 29 HRA or were sold in the judicial sale; it is undisputed 604 is subject to use restrictions in the Incentive Agreement.

propositions.text: Heritage and LBI argue HRA does not allow Incentive Payments to run with the land; payments are contractual and not intended to run with land.
propositions.quote: Heritage is supported by LBI in its argument that the HRA does not allow the Incentive Payments to run with the land, that the right to the Incentive Payments is merely contractual and that the parties to the Incentive Agreement never intended these payments to run with the land.

propositions.text: Heritage argues Incentive Payments were not sold in the judicial sale and it has priority due to earlier PPSA registration.
propositions.quote: It also submits that the Incentive Payments were not sold as an asset in the judicial sale. Therefore, Heritage argues that as a creditor to LBI, it was assigned the Incentive Payments as security, and that it has priority with respect to these payments because its security was registered under the PPSA first.

paragraphs.summary: Heritage and LBI argue Incentive Payments are contractual, not running with land, not sold in judicial sale, and Heritage has priority by earlier PPSA registration.

propositions.text: Master Laycock declared Incentive Payments were not an interest in land.
propositions.quote: Master Laycock granted the order sought by LBI, declaring that the Incentive Payments were not an interest in land.

propositions.text: HRA scheme requires City to compensate owner at time of designation; payments intended as purely contractual benefit to LBI.
propositions.quote: In his view, the scheme of the HRA required the City to compensate the owner of the property at the time the land or building was designated a historic resource. He concluded that the parties to the Incentive Agreement had intended the Incentive Payments to be a purely contractual benefit that was to be bestowed on LBI.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments were not sold to 604 as an asset in judicial sale; no indication in claim, order or listing.
propositions.quote: He further declared that the Incentive Payments had not been sold to 604 as an asset in the judicial sale. He found that neither Equitable’s statement of claim nor the order for sale of the Lougheed Building nor the judicial sale listing indicated that the court intended to include the payments in the judicial sale.

paragraphs.summary: Master Laycock found Incentive Payments not an interest in land, intended as contractual benefit to LBI, and not sold to 604 in judicial sale.

propositions.text: No mention of Incentive Payments in 604 Offer or court acceptance.
propositions.quote: The master further noted that there was no mention of the Incentive Payments in the 604 Offer or in the court’s acceptance of the offer.

propositions.text: Equitable’s claim referred to general security including personal property connected to the land, but Incentive Payments did not fall within that description.
propositions.quote: Equitable’s statement of claim referred to its general security agreement, which included personal property “located at or used in connection with the property”, but he was of the view that the Incentive Payments did not fall within that description of the property.

propositions.text: 604 Assignment executed after sale was ineffective as debt had not been transferred and payments were collateral only.
propositions.quote: With respect to the 604 Assignment, which had been executed after the sale of the Lougheed Building, the master held that because the Incentive Payments were only collateral for the debt and the debt had not been transferred, the transfer of the interest in the Incentive Payments was ineffective.

paragraphs.summary: Master found no mention of payments in 604 Offer or claim; payments not personal property connected to land; 604 Assignment ineffective as debt not transferred.

propositions.text: Chambers judge dismissed 604’s appeal, declaring LBI entitled to Incentive Payments as of August 30, 2010.
propositions.quote: The chambers judge, Jeffrey J., dismissed 604’s appeal of the master’s order, declaring that LBI had been entitled to receive the Incentive Payments as at August 30, 2010.

propositions.text: s. 29(3) HRA does not allow Incentive Payments to run with land as positive covenant; only covenants in favour of City run with land.
propositions.quote: He found that s. 29(3) of the HRA did not operate such that the Incentive Payments could run with the land as a positive covenant, given that only covenants in favour of the City can run with the land under that provision.

propositions.text: HRA scheme requires City to compensate owner at designation time; payments do not run with land, consistent with parties’ intention.
propositions.quote: Jeffrey J. agreed with the master’s conclusion that the scheme of the HRA is to require the City to compensate the owner of property at the time of a designation under s. 26. In his view, the conclusion that the City’s covenant to pay did not run with the land was consistent with the apparent intention of the parties to the Incentive Agreement.

propositions.text: If Incentive Payments were assets sold, 604 Offer would have expressly referred to them.
propositions.quote: Regarding the judicial sale, he found that if the right to receive the Incentive Payments were an asset included in the sale, the 604 Offer would have expressly referred to it.

propositions.text: Declined to decide PPSA priority issue as 604 Assignment executed after August 30, 2010, beyond scope of issues before him.
propositions.quote: He declined to decide the issue with respect to the PPSA priorities, finding that because the 604 Assignment had been executed after August 30, 2010, it was beyond the scope of the issues properly before him.

paragraphs.summary: Chambers judge dismissed 604’s appeal, found payments do not run with land under s.29(3), payments not sold in judicial sale, and declined PPSA priority issue.

propositions.text: Proper standard for reviewing chambers judge’s interpretation of HRA, Incentive Agreement, and 604 Offer is correctness.
propositions.quote: The majority held that the proper standard for reviewing the chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA, the Incentive Agreement and the 604 Offer was correctness.

propositions.text: HRA creates sui generis historic resource covenant that runs fully with the land.
propositions.quote: They found that the HRA creates a sui generis historic resource covenant that runs fully with the land.

propositions.text: s. 29 should be read as displacing common law restrictions on positive covenants running with land, not limited to covenants in favour of City.
propositions.quote: In their view, s. 29 should be read as setting aside all common law restrictions that prohibit positive covenants from running with the land and should not be interpreted as allowing only positive covenants in favour of the City.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement cannot be severed to separate building-related covenants from payment-related covenants.
propositions.quote: The majority also found that the Incentive Agreement could not be severed such that the portions of it relating directly to the building could run with the land but the portions relating to the payments could not.

paragraphs.summary: Majority held standard of review is correctness; HRA creates historic resource covenant running with land; s.29 displaces common law limits on positive covenants; Incentive Agreement inseparable.

propositions.text: Omission of Incentive Agreement in Equitable’s claim does not imply forfeiture of security portion.
propositions.quote: The majority concluded that the omission of a specific reference to the Incentive Agreement in Equitable’s statement of claim should not be taken to imply that it had decided to forego a portion of its security.

propositions.text: Receivership order included the Incentive Agreement.
propositions.quote: They noted that the receivership order issued by the court on consent included the Incentive Agreement.

propositions.text: 604 agreed to take on burdens of Incentive Agreement by taking title subject to caveat; payments and obligations inseparable.
propositions.quote: In their view, 604 had clearly agreed to take on the burdens of the Incentive Agreement — it had taken title subject to the caveat protecting the historic resource covenants — and nothing in the Incentive Agreement suggested that the payments could or would be separated from the obligations under the agreement.

propositions.text: Payments are conditional on performance of obligations; it is illogical to pass burdens but not benefits with sale.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the majority found that the payments were clearly conditional on the performance of the obligations in the agreement and, all things considered, it did not make sense to suggest that the burdens of the Incentive Agreement had passed with the sale, but not the benefits.

paragraphs.summary: Majority found omission of Incentive Agreement in claim does not forgo security; receivership included it; 604 took title subject to burdens and benefits inseparable.

propositions.text: Interpretation of HRA and common law principles is correctness standard; application and agreement interpretation is palpable and overriding error standard.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. held that the chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA and common law principles were matters of law for which the appropriate standard was correctness, whereas his application of the legal principles and interpretation of the agreements were matters of mixed fact and law for which the standard was palpable and overriding error, and therefore required deference.

propositions.text: HRA ensures covenants by landowner in favour of City run with land; does not permit positive covenants in favour of landowner to run with land.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. was of the view that the objective of the HRA is to ensure that covenants made by a landowner in favour of the City, whether positive or negative, run with the land and are enforceable against all subsequent owners, but that the HRA does not permit positive covenants in favour of the landowner to run with the land.

propositions.text: Parties to Incentive Agreement did not intend Incentive Payments to run with the land.
propositions.quote: Further, in his view, the parties to the Incentive Agreement did not intend the Incentive Payments to run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: Dissenting judge held correctness standard for HRA interpretation, deference for application; HRA allows covenants in favour of City to run with land, not positive covenants in favour of landowner; payments not intended to run with land.

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement was not included in 604 Offer; no express statement or indication of inclusion in sale documents.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. held that the Incentive Agreement was not included in the 604 Offer. He noted that the 604 Offer did not state expressly that the payments under the Incentive Agreement were among the property and assets included in the sale, and there was no indication of an intention to this effect in the documents related to the sale.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal was not positioned to determine entitlement to Incentive Payments given scope and evidentiary record.
propositions.quote: Regarding the order of priorities, O’Brien J.A. found that, having regard to the scope of the original application and to the evidentiary record, the Court of Appeal was not in a position to determine who was entitled to the Incentive Payments at that time.

paragraphs.summary: Dissent found Incentive Agreement not included in 604 Offer and Court of Appeal could not determine entitlement to payments given record and scope.

propositions.text: What is the standard of review for chambers judge’s interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer?
propositions.quote: (1) What is the standard of review applicable to the chambers judge’s interpretation of the Incentive Agreement and the 604 Offer?

propositions.text: Did the Incentive Payments run with the land?
propositions.quote: (2) Did the Incentive Payments run with the land?

propositions.text: Does s. 29 of the HRA displace common law rule that positive covenants do not run with the land?
propositions.quote: (a) Does s. 29 of the HRA displace the common law rule that positive covenants do not run with the land?

propositions.text: Does the Incentive Agreement show parties intended Incentive Payments to run with the land?
propositions.quote: (b) Does the Incentive Agreement registered on title show that the parties to the agreement intended the Incentive Payments to run with the land?

propositions.text: Were the Incentive Payments sold as an asset in the judicial sale?
propositions.quote: (3) Were the Incentive Payments sold as an asset in the judicial sale?

propositions.text: Is priority of interests in Incentive Payments governed by the PPSA?
propositions.quote: (4) Is the priority of interests in the Incentive Payments governed by the PPSA?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies four issues: standard of review, whether payments run with land including s.29 and intent, whether payments were sold in judicial sale, and whether PPSA governs priority.

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation involves mixed fact and law, applying principles to contract words in factual context.
propositions.quote: contractual interpretation involves issues of mixed fact and law as it is an exercise in which the principles of contractual interpretation are applied to the words of the written contract, considered in light of the factual matrix

propositions.text: Deference to fact finders in contractual interpretation limits appeals and promotes trial autonomy and integrity.
propositions.quote: deference to fact finders furthers the goals of limiting the number, length and cost of appeals, and of promoting the autonomy and integrity of trial proceedings

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation should be treated as mixed fact and law, with deference to first-instance decision makers.
propositions.quote: These principles weigh in favour of showing deference to first-instance decision makers on points of contractual interpretation, and treating contractual interpretation as a question of mixed fact and law

paragraphs.summary: The court states contractual interpretation involves mixed fact and law, requiring deference to first-instance decision makers to limit appeals and promote trial integrity.

propositions.text: Where an extricable question of law exists, the correctness standard applies in review.
propositions.quote: where an extricable question of law can be identified, the standard of correctness applies

propositions.text: Extricable questions of law include incorrect principle application, failure to consider legal test elements or relevant factors.
propositions.quote: Extricable questions of law include “the application of an incorrect principle, the failure to consider a required element of a legal test, or the failure to consider a relevant factor”

paragraphs.summary: The court states correctness standard applies to extricable questions of law, including incorrect principle application or failure to consider legal test elements.

propositions.text: 604 argues chambers judge erred interpreting HRA, tainting Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer interpretation, requiring correctness standard.
propositions.quote: the chambers judge in the case at bar erred in interpreting the HRA and this tainted his interpretation of the Incentive Agreement and the 604 Offer, which means that the applicable standard of review for the latter interpretation is correctness

propositions.text: Court disagrees; correctness applies to HRA statutory interpretation but not to contractual interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer.
propositions.quote: correctness is the appropriate standard for reviewing the chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA given that statutory interpretation is a question of law... we do not find that this standard applies to his contractual interpretation of the Incentive Agreement and the 604 Offer

propositions.text: Chambers judge’s interpretation of HRA was correct and did not taint contractual interpretation of agreements.
propositions.quote: As the chambers judge’s interpretation of the HRA was correct, it did not taint the interpretation of the agreements

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues chambers judge erred on HRA interpretation tainting contract interpretation; the court disagrees, finding HRA interpretation correct and no taint.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. correctly concluded correctness standard applies to HRA and common law interpretation.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. was right to conclude that the correctness standard applies to the interpretation of the HRA and the common law

propositions.text: Palpable and overriding error standard applies to chambers judge’s interpretation of Incentive Agreement and 604 Offer.
propositions.quote: the palpable and overriding error standard applies to the chambers judge’s interpretation of the Incentive Agreement and the 604 Offer

paragraphs.summary: The court finds O’Brien J.A. correctly applied correctness standard to HRA and common law, and palpable error standard to contractual interpretation.

propositions.text: Payment obligations running with land are unusual; common law disallows positive covenants running with land.
propositions.quote: it is undisputed that at common law, positive covenants cannot run with the land

propositions.text: Common law rule: a person cannot be liable on contract unless party to it, barring positive covenants running with land.
propositions.quote: a person cannot be made liable upon a contract unless he or she was party to it

propositions.text: Rule against positive covenants running with land applies even if agreement expresses contrary intention.
propositions.quote: The rule against positive covenants running with the land applies even if an agreement contains an express intention to the contrary

propositions.text: No personal or affirmative covenant requiring money or act can run with land apart from statute.
propositions.quote: No personal or affirmative covenant, requiring the expenditure of money or the doing of some act, can, apart from statute, be made to run with the land

propositions.text: Issue is whether s. 29 of HRA displaces common law rule by permitting positive covenants to run with land.
propositions.quote: The issue in the instant case is whether and to what extent s. 29 of the HRA displaces the common law rule by permitting positive covenants to run with the land

paragraphs.summary: The court explains common law disallows positive covenants running with land and poses issue whether s. 29 HRA displaces this rule.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. and chambers judge properly interpreted s. 29 HRA limiting positive covenants running with land to those in favour of listed entities.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. and the chambers judge properly interpreted the HRA. We find that s. 29 of the HRA limits the positive covenants that may run with the land to those that are in favour of the City or of the other person or organizations listed in s. 29(1)

propositions.text: HRA does not permit positive covenants in favour of entities not listed in s. 29(1) to run with the land.
propositions.quote: The HRA does not permit positive covenants in favour of an entity not listed in s. 29(1) to run with the land

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 29 HRA limits positive covenants running with land to those favouring listed entities and excludes others.

propositions.text: Modern statutory interpretation requires reading s. 29 HRA in context, ordinary sense, harmonizing with Act’s scheme and purpose.
propositions.quote: Applying the widely accepted modern approach to statutory interpretation, we find that the words of s. 29 of the HRA, when read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act and the intention of Parliament

propositions.text: Only covenants in favour of persons or organizations listed in s. 29(1), positive or negative, run with the land under HRA.
propositions.quote: only covenants in favour of a “person or organization” listed in s. 29(1), whether negative or positive, will run with the land

propositions.text: In this case, right to Incentive Payments did not become an interest running with land by virtue of HRA.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, therefore, the right to the Incentive Payments did not become an interest that runs with the land by virtue of the HRA

paragraphs.summary: The court applies modern statutory interpretation to hold only covenants favouring listed persons run with land; Incentive Payments do not run with land here.

propositions.text: Statutory provisions are presumed to work together as parts of a functioning whole, forming an internally consistent framework.
propositions.quote: there is a presumption of statutory interpretation that the provisions of a statute are meant to work together “as parts of a functioning whole”

propositions.text: Each legal provision should be considered in relation to others as parts of a whole.
propositions.quote: each legal provision should be considered in relation to other provisions, as parts of a whole

paragraphs.summary: The court cites presumption that statutory provisions work together as a consistent whole, each considered in relation to others.

propositions.text: Legislature presumed not to change existing law or principles unless done clearly and unambiguously.
propositions.quote: the presumption that the legislature does not intend to change existing law or to depart from established principles, policies or practices

propositions.text: Legislature must express intention with irresistible clearness to depart from general law system.
propositions.quote: a Legislature is not presumed to depart from the general system of the law without expressing its intentions to do so with irresistible clearness

propositions.text: In absence of clear provision, legislator not assumed to alter pre-existing common law rules.
propositions.quote: in the absence of a clear provision to the contrary, the legislator should not be assumed to have intended to alter the pre‑existing ordinary rules of common law

paragraphs.summary: The court cites presumption that legislature does not change existing law unless clearly and unambiguously expressed.

propositions.text: Legislation must show clear intention to displace common law rules.
propositions.quote: to displace a common law rule, the legislation must show a clear intention to do so

propositions.text: Statutes should not be construed to alter common law or established principles unless clearly intended.
propositions.quote: statutes should not be construed so as to make any alteration in the common law or to change any established principle of law

paragraphs.summary: The court cites that statutes must clearly intend to displace common law and not alter it ambiguously.

propositions.text: Exception to common law in s. 29 HRA should be limited by precise language and purpose of HRA.
propositions.quote: the exception to the common law rule provided for in s. 29 of the HRA should be limited by the precise language of the provision and the underlying purpose of the HRA

propositions.text: Section 29 should not be interpreted more broadly than necessary; positive covenants enforceable only by listed entities.
propositions.quote: Section 29 should not be interpreted more broadly than necessary. The express words of the enactment state that while positive covenants may run with the land, they are enforceable only by the entities listed in s. 29(1)

propositions.text: Purposive and contextual analysis shows HRA does not have broader reach by necessary implication.
propositions.quote: A purposive and contextual analysis of the HRA, and particularly of s. 29, shows that the legislation does not have a broader reach by necessary implication

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 29 HRA exception to common law is limited to precise language and purpose, not broader than necessary.

propositions.text: Section 2 HRA assigns Minister responsibility for coordination, preservation, study, interpretation, and promotion of Alberta’s historic resources.
propositions.quote: Section 2 of the HRA provides that the Minister is responsible for “(a) the co-ordination of the orderly development, (b) the preservation, (c) the study and interpretation, and (d) the promotion of appreciation of Alberta’s historic resources”

propositions.text: Historic resource defined broadly to include natural and human works of palaeontological, archaeological, historic, cultural, scientific, or esthetic interest.
propositions.quote: A “historic resource” is defined as “any work of nature or of humans that is primarily of value for its palaeontological, archaeological, prehistoric, historic, cultural, natural, scientific or esthetic interest

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 2 HRA assigns Minister responsibility for historic resources, broadly defined to include natural and human works of interest.

propositions.text: Section 26(2) HRA allows municipalities to designate Municipal Historic Resources by bylaw.
propositions.quote: Section 26(2) of the HRA provides that a municipality may by bylaw designate any historic resource within the municipality as a “Municipal Historic Resource”

propositions.text: Section 28(1) HRA entitles owner to compensation if bylaw decreases economic value of designated building or land.
propositions.quote: Section 28(1) then provides that if a bylaw under s. 26 decreases the economic value of the building or land designated by the bylaw, the owner of the building or land is entitled to compensation for the decrease

propositions.text: Section 28 does not specify compensation right for future owners nor refer to s. 29, supporting interpretation that compensation is for owner at designation time.
propositions.quote: Section 28 does not specify that the right to compensation is available to a future owner, nor does it refer to s. 29, which supports the chambers judge’s interpretation to the effect that the intended recipient of the compensation under s. 28 is the owner at the time of the designation

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 26(2) allows municipal designation and s. 28(1) entitles owner to compensation, intended for owner at designation time.

propositions.text: Section 29 HRA details conditions or covenants relating to preservation or restoration entered by owner and specified entities, registrable with Land Titles.
propositions.quote: 29(1) A condition or covenant, relating to the preservation or restoration of any land or building, entered into by the owner of land and (a) the Minister, (b) the council of the municipality in which the land is located, (c) the Foundation, or (d) an historical organization that is approved by the Minister, may be registered with the Registrar of Land Titles

propositions.text: Registrar must endorse memorandum of condition or covenant on certificate of title when presented for registration under s. 29(2).
propositions.quote: When a condition or covenant under subsection (1) is presented for registration, the Registrar of Land Titles shall endorse a memorandum of the condition or covenant on any certificate of title relating to that land

propositions.text: Registered condition or covenant runs with land and may be enforced by listed person or organization, positive or negative, even without land interest.
propositions.quote: A condition or covenant registered under subsection (2) runs with the land and the person or organization under subsection (1) that entered into the condition or covenant with the owner may enforce it whether it is positive or negative in nature and notwithstanding that the person or organization does not have an interest in any land

propositions.text: Registered condition or covenant may be assigned by listed person or organization to others listed in s. 29(1), with enforcement rights transferred.
propositions.quote: A condition or covenant registered under subsection (2) may be assigned by the person or organization that entered into it with the owner to any other person or organization mentioned in subsection (1), and the assignee may enforce the condition or covenant as if it were the person or organization that entered into the condition or covenant with the owner

propositions.text: Minister may discharge or modify registered condition or covenant by order if in public interest, regardless of party status.
propositions.quote: If the Minister considers it in the public interest to do so, the Minister may by order discharge or modify a condition or covenant registered under subsection (2), whether or not the Minister is a party to the condition or covenant

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes s. 29 HRA provisions on registration, enforcement, assignment, and Minister’s power over preservation covenants.

propositions.text: Court agrees with chambers judge and O’Brien J.A. that s. 29 subsections form coherent whole allowing listed entities to register and enforce preservation covenants.
propositions.quote: We agree with the chambers judge’s interpretation of the above provision, which O’Brien J.A. accepted. Each subsection of s. 29 is like a piece of a puzzle, and when they are all read together, they form a coherent whole

propositions.text: Section 29(1) allows registration of preservation covenants entered by owner and listed entities.
propositions.quote: Section 29(1) provides that a condition or covenant “relating to the preservation or restoration of any land or building” that is entered into by a landowner and the Minister or one of the organizations enumerated there may be registered

propositions.text: Section 29(3) provides registered covenants run with land and can be enforced by listed persons or organizations, positive or negative.
propositions.quote: Section 29(3) provides that a condition or covenant registered under s. 29(2) runs with the land and can, whether it is negative or positive, be enforced by the “person or organization” listed in s. 29(1)

propositions.text: Subsections (1) and (3) necessary for preservation of Municipal Historic Resources, enabling City enforcement despite lack of land interest.
propositions.quote: Subsections (1) and (3) are necessary for the preservation or restoration of Municipal Historic Resources, because without them, the City would not be able to enforce such a covenant or condition at common law, as it would have no interest in the land or building to which the covenant or condition applied

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees s. 29 subsections form a coherent whole allowing listed entities to register and enforce preservation covenants.

propositions.text: Section 29(3) does not expressly grant landowner ability to enforce condition or covenant against City.
propositions.quote: It is noteworthy that s. 29(3) does not expressly grant a landowner the ability to enforce a condition or covenant against the City

propositions.text: 604 argues express language unnecessary as landowner can enforce covenants due to land interest.
propositions.quote: According to 604, express language to this effect is unnecessary, because the landowner can already enforce covenants and conditions, given that he or she has an interest in the land or building

propositions.text: Court finds legislature would have expressly stated if intending to create covenants enforceable by both City and landowner.
propositions.quote: In our view, had the legislature intended to completely displace the common law rules regarding positive covenants and create sui generis covenants and conditions that are enforceable by both the City and the landowner, it would have said so expressly

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 29(3) does not grant landowner enforcement rights against City; 604 argues otherwise but court rejects it.

propositions.text: 604 argues s. 29(2) allows owner to register covenants and thus enforce them under HRA despite no express wording in s. 29(3).
propositions.quote: An additional submission by 604 is that s. 29(2), which does not on its face prevent the owner from registering a covenant or condition on title, shows that the owner can register covenants, and therefore can also enforce them under the HRA

propositions.text: Court rejects 604’s argument, reading s. 29(3) conjunctively to limit enforcement to listed persons or organizations.
propositions.quote: we are not convinced by this argument. In our view, s. 29(3) should be read as a whole, and the word “and” in that provision should be considered to be conjunctive rather than disjunctive

propositions.text: Section 29(3) specifies enforcement by listed persons or organizations who entered into covenant, not owners.
propositions.quote: Section 29(3) provides that ... the person or organization under subsection (1) that entered into the condition or covenant with the owner may enforce it whether it is positive or negative

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues owner can register and enforce covenants under s. 29; court rejects, reading s. 29(3) as limiting enforcement to listed entities.

propositions.text: Subsections following s. 29(3) further confirm court’s interpretation limiting enforcement rights.
propositions.quote: The two subsections immediately following s. 29(3) further confirm our interpretation

paragraphs.summary: The court notes subsections following s. 29(3) confirm its interpretation limiting enforcement rights.

propositions.text: Section 29(4) allows assignment of registered covenants by listed persons or organizations to others listed in s. 29(1).
propositions.quote: s. 29(4) provides that a condition or covenant registered under s. 29(2) can be assigned by the “person or organization” to any other “person or organization” mentioned in s. 29(1)

propositions.text: No mention in s. 29(4) of landowner’s ability to assign any condition or covenant.
propositions.quote: there is no mention in s. 29(4) of the landowner being able to assign any “condition or covenant”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 29(4) allows assignment of covenants only by listed persons, not landowners.

propositions.text: Section 29 intended to permit governments and public interest bodies without land interest to enforce covenants in their favour.
propositions.quote: this is further evidence that s. 29 is intended to permit governments and public interest bodies that have no interest in the land or building to enforce covenants and conditions that are in their favour

propositions.text: Legislature avoids superfluous words and does not speak in vain; every statute provision should have meaning and function.
propositions.quote: there is a presumption that the legislature “avoids superfluous or meaningless words, that it does not pointlessly repeat itself or speak in vain”

propositions.text: Courts should avoid interpretations rendering any statute portion meaningless, pointless or redundant.
propositions.quote: courts should avoid, as much as possible, adopting interpretations that would render any portion of a statute meaningless or pointless or redundant

propositions.text: Section 29(4) ensures City can assign registered covenants to others listed in s. 29(1) who may enforce them as original parties.
propositions.quote: Section 29(4) ensures that the City can assign a condition or covenant registered under s. 29(2) to any other person or organization mentioned in s. 29(1), such that the assignee may enforce the condition or covenant as if it were the person or organization that entered into the condition or covenant with the owner

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 29 intended to allow governments and public bodies to enforce covenants, with assignment rights ensuring meaningful statute provisions.

propositions.text: Minister may discharge or modify a covenant under s. 29(5) only if covenant is in favour of a person or organization under s. 29(1).
propositions.quote: s. 29(5) provides that the Minister may at any time discharge or modify a covenant or condition registered under s. 29(2) if it is in the public interest to do so.

propositions.text: Minister cannot unilaterally discharge a covenant to pay in favour of a landowner just because of public interest.
propositions.quote: it would be unjust if the Minister could unilaterally discharge a covenant to pay in favour of a landowner simply because he or she considered it in the public interest to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 29(5) allows Minister to discharge covenants only if in favour of persons under s. 29(1), not landowners, to avoid injustice.

propositions.text: Covenants enforceable under s. 29(3) are those in favour of persons or organizations listed in s. 29(1).
propositions.quote: the covenants and conditions that may be enforced under s. 29(3) are those that the “person or organization” listed in s. 29(1) can in fact enforce: the covenants and conditions in its favour.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes covenants enforceable under s. 29(3) benefit persons or organizations in s. 29(1).

propositions.text: Incentive Agreement does not show intention that Incentive Payments run with the land; no basis to disturb chambers judge's findings.
propositions.quote: the Incentive Agreement itself does not reveal an intention that the Incentive Payments would run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Incentive Agreement does not show intention for payments to run with the land, upholding chambers judge's findings.

propositions.text: Clauses 5.3, 8.3 and 8.8 of the Incentive Agreement are primarily at issue.
propositions.quote: The provisions of the Incentive Agreement that are primarily at issue are clauses 5.3, 8.3 and 8.8.

propositions.text: Clause 5.3 allows City to set off unpaid taxes by owner or future owner against amounts owed to owner by City.
propositions.quote: Clause 5.3 states: If, at any time, the Owner, The Lougheed Block Inc., and any future owner, has not paid such taxes and levies when they become due, the City may, but is not obligated to, set off the amount owed by the Owner, the Lougheed Block Inc., or any future owner against any amounts owed, or that may be owing in the future, to the Owner by the City pursuant to this Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies clauses 5.3, 8.3, and 8.8 as key, noting clause 5.3's set-off provision involving owners and future owners.

propositions.text: Clause 5.3 does not show parties intended Incentive Payments to go to future owner; only taxes references future owners.
propositions.quote: The clause does not refer to a future owner when describing the recipient of the payments from the City under the agreement.

propositions.text: No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation of clause 5.3.
propositions.quote: We find no palpable and overriding error in this interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with chambers judge that clause 5.3 does not intend payments to future owners and finds no error in that interpretation.

propositions.text: Clause 8.3 restates s. 29 of HRA about covenants running with land enforceable by City.
propositions.quote: he found that this was simply a restatement of what is provided for in s. 29 of the HRA (enforcement by the City of a positive or negative covenant in its own favour).

propositions.text: No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation of clause 8.3; reference to s. 29 does not show intention for payments to run with land.
propositions.quote: Again, we find no palpable and overriding error in this interpretation. The reference to s. 29 does not show that the parties to the agreement intended the Incentive Payments to run with the land.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds clause 8.3 merely restates s. 29 HRA and does not show intention for payments to run with land, upholding chambers judge.

propositions.text: Clause 8.8 binds parties, their administrators, successors, and assigns; 604 is not an administrator, successor or assign of LBI.
propositions.quote: According to the master’s interpretation, 604, which was merely a subsequent owner, cannot be considered an administrator, successor or assign of LBI.

propositions.text: Contracting parties are presumed to intend legal consequences of their words; different terms in clauses have distinct meanings.
propositions.quote: Contracting parties are presumed to intend the legal consequences of their words

propositions.text: Intention was that LBI alone, after rehabilitation, was entitled to Incentive Payments over 15 years.
propositions.quote: the intention of the contracting parties was that LBI alone would, after completing the rehabilitation work, be entitled to the Incentive Payments, which were to be paid over 15 years.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds 604 is not a successor or assign of LBI; parties intended only LBI to receive Incentive Payments after rehabilitation.

propositions.text: 604 argues it is illogical to sever benefits (Incentive Payments) from burdens (restrictions) under Incentive Agreement.
propositions.quote: In 604’s submission, it would not make sense to sever the benefits available to the owner under the Incentive Agreement... from the burdens imposed on it

propositions.text: Nothing unusual about severing Incentive Payments from burdens related to Municipal Historic Resource restrictions.
propositions.quote: there is nothing unusual about severing the Incentive Payments, a benefit under the Incentive Agreement, from the burdens relating to certain restrictions flowing from the designation of the building as a Municipal Historic Resource.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues benefits and burdens under the Incentive Agreement should not be severed; the court disagrees, finding no unusualness in severing them.

propositions.text: Clause 5.3 does not confirm payments intended for future owner; reasonable interpretation is all payments intended for LBI.
propositions.quote: nothing in clause 5.3 confirms that the parties to the Incentive Agreement intended the payments to go to a future owner.

propositions.text: Recitals and clauses 3, 4, and 5.4 support conclusion that LBI was entitled to all Incentive Payments.
propositions.quote: the recitals of the Incentive Agreement, together with clauses 3 (Rehabilitation Work), 4 (Payment of Rehabilitation Incentive) and 5.4, lead to the conclusion that LBI was entitled to receive all of the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds clause 5.3 and other provisions show LBI was entitled to all Incentive Payments, not future owners.

propositions.text: LBI was owner at designation, completed rehabilitation, suffered loss, and paid for rehabilitation benefiting 604 as new owner.
propositions.quote: it is LBI that was the owner at the time of the designation and that completed all of the rehabilitative work 604 now benefits from as the new owner.

propositions.text: 604 could consider designation when purchasing; payments to future owner would lack commercial rationale and give 604 undeserved windfall.
propositions.quote: to conclude now that the intention was for the Incentive Payments to go to a future owner would have no commercial rationale and would, in essence, provide 604 with an undeserved windfall.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds LBI was the rehabilitating owner and payments to future owner lack commercial rationale, preventing 604's windfall.

propositions.text: 604 submits it purchased right to Incentive Payments in judicial sale.
propositions.quote: Another submission by 604 is that it purchased the right to the Incentive Payments in the judicial sale.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; chambers judge's conclusion that Incentive Payments were not sold in judicial sale is well supported.
propositions.quote: we disagree. The chambers judge’s conclusion that the Incentive Payments were not sold in the judicial sale is well supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues it bought Incentive Payments in judicial sale; court disagrees, supporting chambers judge's conclusion.

propositions.text: 604 Offer defines 'Property' as Lougheed Building legal description; lists fixtures, equipment, chattels owned by vendor as ancillary property.
propositions.quote: the “Property” being purchased is defined using the legal description of the Lougheed Building (the real property) alone... 10. All fixtures, equipment and chattels located on the Property and which are owned by the Vendor shall be included in the Purchase Price.

propositions.text: Fixtures owned by tenants are excluded from sale.
propositions.quote: The Purchaser acknowledges that certain of said fixtures, equipment and chattels are the property of the tenants of the Property and are not included in the sale hereunder.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes 604 Offer's property definition and ancillary property, excluding tenant-owned fixtures.

propositions.text: 604 Offer states assignable leases and contracts shall be assigned to purchaser, who assumes obligations.
propositions.quote: [a]ll leases and contracts that are assignable shall be assigned to the Purchaser as of the Closing Date and the Purchaser shall assume all obligations thereunder.

propositions.text: 604 argues Incentive Agreement was an assignable contract and thus sold to 604 in judicial sale.
propositions.quote: In 604’s submission, the Incentive Agreement was an “assignable contract” within the meaning of para. 6 and was therefore sold to 604 in the judicial sale.

paragraphs.summary: 604 argues Incentive Agreement was assignable contract sold to it; court notes offer's assignable contracts clause.

propositions.text: Chambers judge found Incentive Agreement was assignable contract but not sold to 604; para. 6 covers only contracts ancillary to Property.
propositions.quote: The chambers judge accepted that the Incentive Agreement was an “assignable contract”, but concluded that it had not been sold to 604, as para. 6 concerns only contracts that are “ancillary to the Property”

propositions.text: Para. 6 does not expand scope of Property; it addresses transaction process.
propositions.quote: para. 6 does not expand the scope of the “Property” being acquired; rather, it merely addresses the process for the transaction.

propositions.text: If 604 intended to purchase Incentive Payments, offer would have expressly mentioned them in Property definition or ancillary property list.
propositions.quote: if 604 had intended to purchase the Incentive Payments, its offer would have expressly mentioned them either in the initial definition of the “Property” or in the list of ancillary property at para. 10.

paragraphs.summary: Chambers judge found Incentive Agreement assignable but not sold to 604; para. 6 limited to ancillary contracts; no express mention of payments.

propositions.text: No palpable and overriding error in chambers judge's interpretation limiting para. 6 to ancillary contracts.
propositions.quote: In our view, the chambers judge did not make a palpable and overriding error in his interpretation of the 604 Offer.

propositions.text: Heritage argues para. 6 limited to ancillary contracts; 604 cannot have purchased all assignable contracts just because they are assignable.
propositions.quote: As Heritage argues, there may have been other contracts to which LBI was a party... 604 cannot be said to have purchased all such contracts just because they were “assignable contracts”.

propositions.text: Given value of Incentive Payments, if 604 intended to purchase them, offer would likely state so expressly; no indication it did.
propositions.quote: Given the substantial value of the Incentive Payments, if 604 had intended to purchase the Incentive Payments, its offer would likely have stated this expressly.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no error in chambers judge's interpretation limiting para. 6; Heritage argues 604 did not purchase all assignable contracts; no express indication of payment purchase.

propositions.text: Statement of claim, judicial sale listing, and marketing brochure did not mention Incentive Agreement or Payments as part of sale.
propositions.quote: the statement of claim initiating the sale proceedings did not refer to the Incentive Agreement or to the Incentive Payments... neither the judicial sale listing nor the marketing brochure... indicated that the Incentive Payments were part of the property and assets included in the judicial sale.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. observed absence of reference to Incentive Agreement or Payments in sale documents.
propositions.quote: As O’Brien J.A. observed, the statement of claim initiating the sale proceedings did not refer to the Incentive Agreement or to the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes sale documents did not mention Incentive Agreement or Payments; O’Brien J.A. observed this absence.

propositions.text: Is priority of interests in Incentive Payments governed by PPSA, given payments do not run with land and were not sold to 604?
propositions.quote: we must now determine whether the assignment of the Incentive Payments is governed by the PPSA.

propositions.text: LBI assigned Incentive Agreement to Equitable and Heritage before default; 604 Assignment executed after sale and registered after Heritage Assignment.
propositions.quote: LBI successively assigned the Incentive Agreement to both Equitable and Heritage before it defaulted on the Equitable loan. The 604 Assignment was executed after the sale of the Lougheed Building... registered at the Personal Property Registry, but not until after the Heritage Assignment had been registered.

paragraphs.summary: Court raises issue whether PPSA governs priority of Incentive Payments; notes LBI's successive assignments and registration timing.

propositions.text: Master Laycock held 604 Assignment ineffective for lack of consideration.
propositions.quote: Master Laycock held that the 604 Assignment was ineffective because no consideration had been paid for it.

propositions.text: Jeffrey J. declined to decide issues of assignments and redemptions, viewing them beyond scope of issue before court.
propositions.quote: Jeffrey J. declined to decide this issue or to address the issues of assignments and redemptions.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority held Incentive Payments ran with land, so PPSA did not apply.
propositions.quote: The majority of the Court of Appeal, having determined that the Incentive Payments ran with the land, held that the PPSA did not apply.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. said Court of Appeal was not in position to determine entitlement to Incentive Payments at that time.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. was of the view that... the Court of Appeal was not in a position to determine which party was entitled to the Incentive Payments at that time.

paragraphs.summary: Master found 604 Assignment ineffective; Jeffrey J. declined to decide; Court of Appeal majority held payments ran with land and PPSA did not apply; O’Brien J.A. dissented.

propositions.text: Heritage argues its Assignment registered before 604's, so it should have priority under PPSA.
propositions.quote: Heritage argues that the Heritage Assignment was registered before the 604 Assignment and that its interest... should therefore have priority under the PPSA.

propositions.text: 604 replies Equitable Assignment was registered before 604 Assignment.
propositions.quote: As for 604, it replies that the Equitable Assignment was already registered under the PPSA at the time of the 604 Assignment.

propositions.text: Heritage says if Court declines PPSA issue, it should at least decide if Incentive Payments are chose in action to facilitate further proceedings.
propositions.quote: Heritage maintains that, should this Court decline to decide the PPSA issue, it should at least determine whether the Incentive Payments are a chose in action so as to facilitate further proceedings between the parties.

paragraphs.summary: Heritage argues its Assignment has priority under PPSA; 604 replies Equitable Assignment registered earlier; Heritage urges Court to decide if payments are chose in action.

propositions.text: PPSA applies to every transaction creating a security interest regardless of form or title to collateral (s. 3(1)(a)).
propositions.quote: The PPSA applies to “every transaction that in substance creates a security interest, without regard to its form and without regard to the person who has title to the collateral” (s. 3(1)(a)).

propositions.text: Incentive Payments are a chose in action, contractual rights not running with land or ancillary to real property.
propositions.quote: We conclude that the Incentive Payments are a chose in action. The right to the Incentive Payments is merely contractual and is not an interest that runs with the land or that is ancillary to the real property.

propositions.text: Interests in Incentive Payments are not exempt from PPSA; PPSA governs priority of interests in them.
propositions.quote: contrary to 604’s suggestion, any interests in the payments are not exempt from the PPSA pursuant to s. 4(f) or (g) thereof. The PPSA governs the priority of interests in the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: Court holds PPSA applies to Incentive Payments as chose in action; payments not exempt; PPSA governs priority of interests.

propositions.text: Jeffrey J. held the Equitable Assignment was only a security interest.
propositions.quote: Jeffrey J. held that the Equitable Assignment was only a security interest.

propositions.text: O’Brien J.A. agreed the assignment was for securing the mortgage debt and was only a security interest.
propositions.quote: O’Brien J.A. accepted Jeffrey J.’s conclusion, as he was also of the view that “the assignment was for purposes of securing the mortgage debt” and that it “constituted a security interest only” (para. 87).

paragraphs.summary: Jeffrey J. and O’Brien J.A. found the Equitable Assignment was only a security interest securing the mortgage debt.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments arise only after LBI completes rehabilitation work and aim to satisfy compensation rights from historic designation and restoration.
propositions.quote: The right to the Incentive Payments, contrary to land lease payments, for example, arose only upon LBI’s completion of the rehabilitation work, and their purpose was to satisfy all rights to compensation from the City that flowed from the historic resource designation and from the restoration.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments were one-time payments to the owner of a newly designated building and not meant to follow the property.
propositions.quote: They were offered on a one-time basis to the owner of a newly designated building and were never meant to follow the property.

propositions.text: Parties agree that if Incentive Payments were lump sum, 604 would not recover part of it, confirming PPSA applies to Incentive Payments.
propositions.quote: This is confirmed by the fact that the parties agree that if the Incentive Payments had been made on a lump sum basis, 604 would not be entitled to recover part of that sum. We are therefore satisfied that the PPSA applies to the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Incentive Payments arise after rehabilitation, are one-time, and PPSA applies to them, as parties agree.

propositions.text: Disagreement on effect of assignments and priorities will be remitted to a master in chambers for decision per court findings.
propositions.quote: to the extent that the parties disagree about the effect of the assignments and the resulting priorities, we would remit this issue alone to a master in chambers to be decided in accordance with our findings above.

propositions.text: Equitable Assignment created only a security interest, so Equitable could only transfer its security interest to 604.
propositions.quote: in light of our conclusion that the Equitable Assignment created a security interest only, the most Equitable could have transferred to 604 was its security interest.

propositions.text: Krayzel Corp. v. Equitable Trust Co. reasons must be considered in further proceedings on Incentive Payments.
propositions.quote: this Court’s reasons in the related appeal, Krayzel Corp. v. Equitable Trust Co., 2016 SCC 18, [2016] 1 S.C.R. 273, which are being issued concurrently with the reasons in this appeal, will have to be considered in any further proceedings relating to the Incentive Payments.

paragraphs.summary: Court remits priority dispute to master; Equitable Assignment only transferred security interest; related Krayzel case must be considered.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed; master’s order restored; costs to Heritage and LBI against 604.
propositions.quote: We would allow the appeal and restore the order of the master in chambers, with costs throughout to Heritage and LBI as against 604.

propositions.text: Incentive Payments under Incentive Agreement are not interests in land under HRA and not assets sold to 604.
propositions.quote: The Incentive Payments arising under the Incentive Agreement are not an interest in land by operation of the HRA and are not among the assets sold to 604.

propositions.text: If parties disagree on PPSA priority between Heritage and 604 Assignments, remit to master for decision per findings.
propositions.quote: If the parties disagree about the order of priorities under the PPSA between the Heritage Assignment and the 604 Assignment, we would remit this issue alone to a master in chambers to be decided in accordance with the foregoing findings.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed with costs; solicitors for parties named.
propositions.quote: Appeal allowed with costs. Solicitors for the appellant: Burnet, Duckworth & Palmer, Calgary. Solicitors for the respondents the Lougheed Block Inc., Neil John Richardson, Hugh Daryl Richardson and the Heritage Property Corporation: Willow Park Law Office, Calgary. Solicitors for the respondent 604 1st Street S.W. Inc.: Gowling WLG (Canada) Inc., Calgary.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal, restores master’s order, finds Incentive Payments not land interests, remits priority dispute, and awards costs.
